verses.128:1: Muitas vezes me {expugnaverunt} desde a minha juventude, * {dicat}.
verses.128:2: Muitas vezes me {expugnaverunt} desde a minha juventude: * {etenim} não puderam comigo.
verses.128:3: Sobre {dorsum} {fabricaverunt} os pecadores: * prolongaram a sua iniquidade.
verses.128:4: {justus} {concidit} {cervices} dos pecadores: * sejam envergonhados e voltem para trás todos os que odeiam Sião.
verses.128:6: Sejam como {fenum} dos telhados: * que, antes de ser {evellatur}, secou:
verses.128:7: {dequo} não encheu a mão {qui_metit}, * nem {sinum} {qui_colligit} os feixes.
verses.128:8: E não disseram os que passavam: A bênção do Senhor {supervos}: * {benediximus} em nome do Senhor.

decisions.why: The same Latin twice, so one wording twice (rule 6). expugnáre / impugnáre are one family (34:1 'expúgna impugnántes me' → 'combatei os que me combatem'), and 108:3 'expugnavérunt me gratis' already reads 'me combateram sem motivo'. The Greek is ἐπολέμησάν, to make war on: 'combater' keeps the war. The Diurnal and the CNBB have 'perseguiram', from the Hebrew (צְרָרוּנִי, 'they distressed me').

options.label: combateram
options.note: Draft. The glossary's verb for this family (34:1, 108:3); the war of the Greek.

options.label: atacaram
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. Plain, but breaks the one verb 34:1 and 108:3 already have.

options.label: perseguiram
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico 1962 and the CNBB Liturgia das Horas ('Quanto eu fui perseguido desde jovem', fetched): the Hebrew's sense, not the Latin's. Refused under rule 1.

decisions.why: A formula: 117:2 'Diga agora Israel' and 123:1 (in parallel, same words). Here it follows what Israel is to say, and 128:2 then repeats it — the Passion Sunday Tract (Quad5-0) even sings 'Dicat nunc Israël: sæpe expugnavérunt me…', so the repetition is what Israel says. The bare formula lets the line point both ways, back to 128:1 and forward to 128:2, as the Latin does.

options.label: diga agora Israel
options.note: Draft. The glossary formula (117:2, 123:1); no object supplied.

options.label: diga-o agora Israel
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The 'o' ties the saying back to 128:1 only, and breaks the formula.

options.label: Israel que o diga
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico 1962's idiom. Lively, but 'que o diga' is colloquial ('just ask Israel'), and 'nunc' is lost.

decisions.why: The glossary's 'étenim → pois' (working) explains. Here nothing is explained: καὶ γάρ stands for the Hebrew גַּם, 'and yet', and after 'they fought me often' 'pois' would be heard as 'because' — 'they fought me often, because they could not overcome me'. The glossary row itself warns (64:14) to watch 'pois' where 'étenim' follows a verb it does not explain. Both Vulgate-family witnesses read it as 'but' (Douay-Rheims 'but they could not prevail over me', Matos Soares 1932 'mas não prevaleceram contra mim').

options.label: mas
options.note: Draft. What DRB and MS1932 hear in this 'étenim'. Cost: a local departure from the glossary row.

options.label: pois
options.note: The glossary's word. Heard as 'because'.

options.label: e
options.note: The 'et' kept and the 'enim' dropped: adds no adversative, but loses the particle's weight.

decisions.why: The literal back. 'costas' is the psalter's word so far (17:41, 20:13, the glossary row 'dare dorsum', which lists 128:3 as the literal back). 'dorso' is Matos Soares's and the CNBB's word here ('Aravam lavradores o meu dorso', fetched), and it is known to Brazilian ears in this psalm; but in current speech it is an animal's back or the back of a hand or a book.

options.label: as minhas costas
options.note: Draft. The plain word for a man's back, and the psalter's word for dorsum (17:41, 20:13). St Bernard read the verse of the scourging (V6.txt), and it is a man's back.

options.label: o meu dorso
options.note: Matos Soares 1932 and the CNBB Liturgia das Horas — the wording Brazilians know from this psalm.

decisions.why: fabricári without an object: the craftsman's verb (L&S 'to make out of wood, stone, metal… frame, forge'; the Greek ἐτέκταινον, the carpenter's or smith's work). The Hebrew has ploughers ploughing (the Diurnal and the CNBB). The glossary's 'fabricári → formar' (73:16) needs an object and cannot stand here. 'Trabalhar' is the one verb that takes no object and keeps the sense of labour done on the back, without saying what the work was — which the Latin does not say either (Augustine's anvil is an interpretation). Draft 2: all three readers found 'trabalharam' too vague; 'forjaram' taken (see its note).

options.label: forjaram
options.note: Draft 2, from the stylist (v1); the Latinist (v1, minor) and the ambiguity reader also found 'trabalharam' generic (heard as 'worked behind my back' or 'loaded their work on me'). The smith's verb, one of fabricári's own senses (L&S 'forge'), and like fabricári it also means to contrive ('forjar uma mentira'), so the Latin's double reach is kept. Used without an object, as the Latin is.

options.label: trabalharam
options.note: Draft 1. Matos Soares 1932; DRB 'wrought'. Three readers found it generic; the image of craft on the back is lost.

options.label: fabricaram
options.note: The Latinist's fix (v1, minor), the cognate. Refused: the 73:16 stylist heard factories in it, and without an object 'fabricaram' is not a Portuguese sentence.

decisions.why: 'justus' stands beside 'Dóminus' as an attribute. The Hebrew reads a predicate ('The Lord is just'), which the CNBB and the Diurnal follow; the Latin does not. Two ways to say the attribute.

options.label: O Senhor, que é justo,
options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's (v1): the comma gives a breath and 'O Senhor justo' in one run sounded like a title. A copula supplied in a relative (rule 2); MS1932 and DRB. +3 syllables (19 against 15).

options.label: O Senhor justo
options.note: Draft 1. Word for word; the stylist found it stiff, like a title.

decisions.why: concīdo (from caedo): 'to cut up, cut to pieces' (L&S). The form concīdit is present and perfect at once. The Greek συνέκοψεν is an aorist, so the perfect; DRB 'will cut' follows another reading. The Tract of Passion Sunday sings it after 'Prolongavérunt iniquitátes suas', where a past reads as God's answer already given.

options.label: cortou
options.note: Draft. The perfect, with the Greek; Matos Soares 1932 'cortou'.

options.label: corta
options.note: The present, which the Latin form also allows.

decisions.why: cervix is the ordinary Latin word for the neck (the nape). 'Cerviz' survives in Brazilian church speech mostly in 'povo de dura cerviz' — the stiff neck of pride, which is the image here too — but its plural 'cervizes' is rarely heard. 'Pescoços' is the plain word and keeps the image concrete (rule 5).

options.label: os pescoços
options.note: Draft. The plainer of two faithful words (rule 2); DRB 'the necks'.

options.label: as cervizes
options.note: Matos Soares 1932. The biblical word, with the echo of 'dura cerviz'; the plural may be unknown to some ears.

decisions.latin: fænum tectórum … quod priúsquam evellátur … De quo
decisions.why: The glossary splits fænum by what the verse does: 'feno' where it is dry (36:2, 101:5, 101:12), 'erva' where it grows (71:16, 91:8, 102:14). Here it is grass growing on the roofs, to be pulled up, which withers first: living grass, so 'erva'. It is also the wording Brazilians know: Matos Soares 1932, the Diurnal and the CNBB all have 'a erva dos telhados' (CNBB fetched). The noun's gender carries into 'arrancada' and 'Da qual'.

options.label: a erva
options.note: Draft. The glossary's split; MS1932, DM1962, CNBB.

options.label: o feno
options.note: The word at 36:2 and 101:12, where it dries. But hay does not grow on roofs, nor is it pulled up.

decisions.latin: De quo non implévit manum suam qui metit, et sinum suum qui manípulos cólligit
decisions.why: The stylist (v1) found 'Da qual' at the head of a new verse a dangling relative the ear cannot tie back, and 'o que ceifa' wavering between 'what he reaps' and 'he who reaps' (the ambiguity reader heard the same and found the order hard). Taken as grammar (D2): the relative 'De quo' becomes the pronoun 'Dela' (the grass; the fenum decision fills it), 'qui metit' becomes 'quem ceifa', and the body part takes the article without the possessive, as Portuguese says it ('encher a mão'). The Latin order and the parallel of the two colons are kept.

options.label: Dela … a mão quem ceifa … quem recolhe
options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's wording; 'suam' and 'suum' are carried by the article.

options.label: Da qual … a sua mão o que ceifa … o que recolhe
options.note: Draft 1 (with 'Da qual' and 'a sua mão'): the relative and both possessives as in the Latin. To restore it wholly, the verse must also read 'Da qual não encheu a sua mão'.

decisions.why: sinus is the fold of the garment at the chest, in which a gatherer carries what he gathers. The glossary has 'seio' (open; 34:13b, 73:11), and the Latin's image is kept. 'Regaço' is the fold of a garment used as a carrier, but in Brazil it is heard first as a lap. Matos Soares's 'braços' is a paraphrase (he marks the verb as his own). Draft 2 takes 'regaço' (see its note).

options.label: regaço
options.note: Draft 2, the stylist's (v1): both the stylist and the ambiguity reader heard 'seio' as the breast. The regaço is the fold of the garment used to carry things (collecting in the regaço is its ordinary use). A local departure from the glossary's 'sinus → seio' (open; 34:13b, 73:11, where the hand is in the bosom and 'seio' still serves). The possessive 'suum' is not repeated, as with 'a mão' (see decision relclause).

options.label: seio
options.note: Draft 1. The glossary's word; DRB 'bosom'. Heard as the breast by two readers.

options.label: os seus braços
options.note: Matos Soares 1932; a paraphrase. Refused: it changes the image (rule 2).

decisions.why: The harvest greeting the passers-by did not give has no verb in the Latin (nor in the Greek). A verbless greeting is sayable in Portuguese and leaves open, as the Latin does, whether it is a wish or a statement. Matos Soares and DRB supply 'seja' / 'be'.

options.label: sobre vós
options.note: Draft. No verb, as the Latin; the colon ends on an oxytone.

options.label: esteja sobre vós
options.note: A copula supplied as a wish (rule 2 allows it); +2 syllables.

options.label: seja sobre vós
options.note: Matos Soares 1932.

decisions.why: Two things. (1) The wording: 117:26b 'Benedíximus vobis de domo Dómini' is already 'Nós vos bendissemos da casa do Senhor' (glossary row 'benedícere (men → men)', open), and identical Latin gets identical Portuguese (rule 6); 'in nómine Dómini' → 'em nome do Senhor' (the row, 117:26a). The CNBB says 'Em nome do Senhor vos bendizemos' (present, fetched); MS1932 'nós vos abençoamos'. The Greek perfect εὐλογήκαμεν can carry a present sense; the Latin form is a perfect. (2) Who speaks: the Latin leaves open whether this colon is still the greeting the passers-by did not give (the reapers' answer, as in Ruth 2:4), or the psalmist's own blessing. No 'but' is supplied, so both readings stay; the Diurnal's 'Mas nós vos abençoamos' closes it.

options.label: nós vos bendissemos
options.note: Draft. 117:26b's words (rule 6); the Latin's perfect; the one verb of 'Benedíctio … benedíximus' kept in one root.

options.label: nós vos bendizemos
options.note: The present of the CNBB Liturgia das Horas (the line Brazilians know) and the Greek perfect's present force; would split from 117:26b.

options.label: nós vos abençoamos
options.note: Matos Soares 1932; the familiar verb, but the benedícere rows keep 'bendizer'.

options.label: mas nós vos bendizemos
options.note: The Diurnal Monástico 1962's reading: the psalmist blesses where the passers-by did not. Refused: it closes an ambiguity the Latin leaves open.

choices.128:1: Per D7 the titulus 'Canticum graduum' is not reproduced (Matos Soares prints 'Cântico gradual'). 'juventus → juventude' as in 42:4 and 24:7 (MS1932 'mocidade'; the CNBB 'desde jovem'). 'sæpe → muitas vezes' as in 105:42. The first colon is sung alone as a Vespers antiphon (Psalmi major, Daya3 Vespera and Monastic Vespera feria 2) and reads alone.
choices.128:2: Identical to 128:1's first colon, word for word, as the Latin repeats. 'non potuérunt mihi' (οὐκ ἠδυνήθησάν μοι) → 'não puderam comigo': the Portuguese idiom 'poder com alguém' is exactly 'to prevail over', and keeps the Latin's bare verb with a pronoun; MS1932's 'prevaleceram contra mim' supplies a stronger verb.
choices.128:3: 'prolongáre → prolongar', as 119:5 'se prolongou' (MS1932 'prolongaram a sua iniquidade'). The Passion Sunday Tract has the plural 'iniquitátes suas'; the psalm's singular is followed. 'os pecadores' after the verb, as in the Latin, puts a paroxytone at the mediant.
choices.128:4: The second colon is DO's verse 5 run in ('(5)' not reproduced). 'confundántur … convertántur retrórsum' → 'sejam envergonhados e voltem para trás': D15's 'confúndi → ser envergonhado' and the glossary row 'retrórsum', which names 128:5 as a place to copy 34:4b ('Voltem para trás, e sejam envergonhados'); here the Latin's order is confundántur first, so the Portuguese follows it. 'odérunt' → present 'odeiam' (the odísse row: a perfect of a state). 'Sion → Sião'. The colon is long (≈22 syllables against the Latin's 20), as the Latin is. The ambiguity reader heard 'cortou os pescoços' as beheading first, and the breaking of pride (the stiff neck) third; the Latin 'concídit cervíces' (cut to pieces the necks) is as violent, and the image is kept.
choices.128:6: 'Fiant sicut' → 'Sejam como' (MS1932, CNBB 'Sejam eles como'). 'exáruit' → 'secou' (arescere → secar, as 36:2, 101:12), kept a perfect and kept at the end of the colon where the Latin puts it. The verse ends in a colon, as the Latin, because 128:7 continues the sentence.
choices.128:7: 'métere → ceifar' and 'manípulus → feixe' as 125:5–6b. 'et' after a negative → 'nem'. The build is decision relclause; the word for sinus is decision sinum.
choices.128:8: 'qui præteríbant' → 'os que passavam' (imperfect; MS1932). The greeting is not set in quotation marks; a capital after the colon marks it, as elsewhere in this psalter (4:6). The addressees of 'vós' are the reapers of 128:7 (plural humans, vós). 'bendissemos' was listed as unknown by the ambiguity reader and heard as a present; kept for 117:26b's identical Latin (decision benediximus, where the present is option 2). Whether 'nós vos bendissemos' continues what was not said or is the psalmist's own blessing stays open, as the reader found it.

audit.note: Psalm-level draft from the parallels (Latin, LXX, Hebrew, DRB, MS1932, DM1962) and the glossary. Liturgical use checked by grep (the Tract of Passion Sunday, the Vespers antiphon, St Bernard's reading of 128:3) and the CNBB wording fetched; see circulation.md. Hard readings: 'étenim' (not causal here), 'fabricavérunt' without an object, 'concídit' present or perfect, 'fænum' living grass, and who speaks in 128:8b.

Hard checks pass. One soft flag, twice: 128:1 and 128:2 first colon +4 syllables (19 against 15). Accepted: 'sæpe' (2) can only be 'muitas vezes' (4), and 'desde a minha juventude' is the Latin's words; dropping 'minha' or taking the CNBB's 'desde jovem' would change the text for the count. The antiphon use (the first colon alone) is not harmed by the length.
claude-opus-5-5, fresh context. One minor (128:3 'trabalharam' generic); the fix 'fabricaram' refused, the complaint met by 'forjaram'.

outcomes.reason: The fault is taken (with the stylist's 'forjaram'); the cognate itself refused — without an object it is not Portuguese, and it was heard as factories at 73:16.

audit.note: claude-opus-5-5, fresh context. Four remarks: three taken, one refused. Best line 128:2, worst 128:7.

outcomes.remark: 'O Senhor justo' stiff; 'O Senhor, que é justo,'
'Da qual' dangling, 'o que ceifa' wavers, redundant possessive; 'Dela não encheu a mão quem ceifa'; 'seio' heard as breast → 'regaço'
set the greeting and the second colon in quotation marks
outcomes.reason: This psalter sets speech after a colon with a capital and no quotation marks (4:6); and quoting the second colon would decide who speaks it, which the Latin leaves open (decision benediximus).

audit.note: claude-opus-5-5, fresh context, blind. 14 ambiguities, 5 unknown words (iniquidade, ceifa, feixes, seio as garment fold, bendissemos).

outcomes.remark: whether the first clause is what Israel says
'trabalharam' heard as 'behind my back' / beast of burden

outcomes.reason: The Latin's image is as violent; kept (choices 128:4); 'as cervizes' is option 2 of decision cervices.

outcomes.remark: 'seio' heard as the breast; 'o que ceifa' as 'what he reaps'; order hard

outcomes.reason: The Latin leaves it open; no 'mas' supplied (decision benediximus).
Identical Latin at 117:26b has 'bendissemos' (rule 6); the present is option 2.

audit.note: v2: 128:3 'forjaram'; 128:4 'O Senhor, que é justo,'; 128:7 'Dela não encheu a mão quem ceifa, * nem o regaço quem recolhe os feixes.' Draft 1 kept as prayed.v1.json.

v2: hard pass. Soft flags accepted: 128:1/128:2 +4 (as v1); 128:4 first colon +3 (the relative the stylist asked for; a comma gives the breath); 128:7 first colon -3 (a short line for a tight image; the second colon is the Latin length).
claude-opus-5-5, fresh context, with latin.json. Gate clean: no remark; it names forjaram, mas for étenim and the dropped possessives of 128:7 as within idiom.
